power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.expanded: Critically, this effect was moderated by group congruence, as shown by a significant interaction between teammate label and group congruence (B = -2.42, SE = 0.68, z = -3.58, p < .001, OR = 0.09, 95% CI [0.02, 0.33]).

When teammates produced dispreferred labels, children were significantly more likely to also use dispreferred labels when their teammates matched their gender compared to when they mismatched (Bgender matching = 1.63, SE = 0.54, z = 3.02, p = .002, OR = 5.12, 95% CI [1.77, 14.77]).

In contrast, when teammates produced preferred labels, children were less likely to produce dispreferred labels when teammates matched their gender (Bgender matching = -0.79, SE = 0.40, z = -1.98, p = .047, OR = 0.46, 95% CI [0.21, 0.99]).

Results showed no evidence of a threeway interaction between child gender, group congruence, and teammate label (B = -1.92, SE = 1.32, z = -1.46, p = .15, OR = 0.15, 95% CI [0.01, 1.95]), suggesting that the interaction we observed between teammate label and group congruence did not differ between boys and girls.

table.formatted: Re-fitting the model with each gender as the reference level, we did find a significant team label × group congruence interaction for girls (B = -3.25, SE = 0.93, z = -3.49, p < .001, OR = 0.04, 95% CI [0.01, 0.24]) but not boys (B = -1.33, SE = 0.94, z = -1.41, p = .16, OR = 0.26, 95% CI [0.04, 1.69]), suggesting that the effect we observed may be driven to some extent by the girls, who showed stronger alignment in the congruent condition compared to the incongruent condition, whereas boys tended to align with their teammates, regardless of whether they mismatched their gender or not (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .15", "p = .16"), Sentence = c("Results showed no evidence of a threeway interaction between child gender, group congruence, and teammate label (B = -1.92, SE = 1.32, z = -1.46, p = .15, OR = 0.15, 95% CI [0.01, 1.95]), suggesting that the interaction we observed between teammate label and group congruence did not differ between boys and girls.", "Re-fitting the model with each gender as the reference level, we did find a significant team label × group congruence interaction for girls (B = -3.25, SE = 0.93, z = -3.49, p < .001, OR = 0.04, 95% CI [0.01, 0.24]) but not boys (B = -1.33, SE = 0.94, z = -1.41, p = .16, OR = 0.26, 95% CI [0.04, 1.69]), suggesting that the effect we observed may be driven to some extent by the girls, who showed stronger alignment in the congruent condition compared to the incongruent condition, whereas boys tended to align with their teammates, regardless of whether they mismatched their gender or not (see Figure 3)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 457 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (444), R history (1), RStudio session files (12). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

#### Code Comments
Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.
#### Missing Files
All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.
#### Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., './files') instead of absolute file paths (e.g., 'C://Lakens/project_dir/files') as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.
#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 76 columns across 10 data files.
#### Issues Identified

14 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 10 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}

    Basis = "none"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 1 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

1 call to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like was replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. info.title: Being a team player: The influence of multiple group memberships on children's lexical choices

author.affiliation:
Institute for Language Sciences
								Utrecht University

Department of Psychology
								University of Toronto

Department of Psychology

Department of Psychology
								University of Toronto

text.text: People use language to signal aspects of their social identity, in part by talking like (i.e., aligning with) those they identify with.
Yet people identify with multiple individuals and groups at once, which may have different (and sometimes conflicting) communication styles that must be reconciled.
Here, we investigated how 7-to 9-year-old children's language choices (whose speech they align with) are shaped by the multiple, sometimes competing groups they belong to.

During the experiment, children (N = 128; 64 cisgender girls and 64 cisgender boys; racially diverse; upper middle class) were assigned to a team (green or yellow) and played a virtual trivia game in which, on critical trials, they answered a question with more than one acceptable answer (e.g., blackboard or chalkboard) after hearing two teammates use one label, and two opponents use the other.

We manipulated (1) whether teammates produced the label more common in the broader community (preferred) or the less common one (dispreferred labels), and (2) whether teammates shared the child's gender (congruent condition) or their opponents did (incongruent condition).
Overall, children aligned with their teammates, producing dispreferred labels more often when their teammates used them.
However, this alignment was attenuated when teammates did not share children's gender, indicating that children weighed both group memberships.
To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that children's lexical alignment is sensitive to the communication patterns of the multiple groups that children belong to.
Part of how we express who we are is by talking like the people and groups we identify with.
But we belong to many groups at once-friends, teams, gender, race, and more.

This study shows that by the age of 7, children adjust their word choices to sound like the multiple groups they belong to, revealing how early they use language in complex ways to signal who they are and where they belong.
One of the primary ways that we express our identity and signal how we relate to others is through language.

During interaction, our accent, the words and grammar that we produce, and how polite or formal our language is, convey which social groups/categories we identify with, and how we perceive our relationship to listeners (see Kinzler, 2021).
text.formatted: During interaction, our accent, the words and grammar that we produce, and how polite or formal our language is, convey which social groups/categories we identify with, and how we perceive our relationship to listeners (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Kinzler, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Part of how we signal who we are is by talking like those we identify with-converging on the words, sounds, and expressions used by other members of our groups (Giles et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Part of how we signal who we are is by talking like those we identify with-converging on the words, sounds, and expressions used by other members of our groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Giles et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Our identities, however, are complex and multifaceted; we simultaneously identify with multiple categories-gender, friendship groups, cliques, and teams-which may carry distinct and sometimes competing communicative norms, commonly experienced, for example, when we try to mix different friend groups, and attempt to reconcile different aspects of our (linguistic) identities.
As children develop, they too must learn to use language flexibly to signal multiple aspects of their identity, and balance these identities when they pull in different directions.
Here, we asked how children's language choices are shaped by the language used by members of the multiple, sometimes competing groups to which they belong.
Because the way we speak signals our identities and which groups we belong to, part of the task of learning to use a language in the long term is figuring out whom to model our speech after.

Children acquire much of language by tracking patterns in their input, but do not indiscriminately reproduce all the patterns that they hear; instead, they are selective about whose speech they emulate.

For example, already by the age of 2, children can be reliably identified by their assigned gender at birth from their voice alone, despite a lack of anatomical differences between boys and girls, suggesting that they align their speech with same-gender individuals (Fung et al., 2021; Wong et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, already by the age of 2, children can be reliably identified by their assigned gender at birth from their voice alone, despite a lack of anatomical differences between boys and girls, suggesting that they align their speech with same-gender individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fung et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Wong et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While children generally appear to pattern their speech early on after their primary caregivers (Chen & Schuler, 2025; Kohn et al., 2020; Smith & Durham, 2019), by the school-aged years, children increasingly align their speech with their peers (Kerswill & Williams, 2000; Smith & Holmes-Elliott, 2022; see also Eckert, 2011), with individual peer groups who interact frequently with one another converging over time (Nardy et al., 2014; see also Mooney, 2020).
text.formatted: While children generally appear to pattern their speech early on after their primary caregivers <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chen & Schuler, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kohn et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Smith & Durham, 2019)</ref>, by the school-aged years, children increasingly align their speech with their peers <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Kerswill & Williams, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Smith & Holmes-Elliott, 2022</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eckert, 2011)</ref>, with individual peer groups who interact frequently with one another converging over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Nardy et al., 2014</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Mooney, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: And when children encounter an entirely new language variety-for example by moving to a region with a different dialect or entering a standardspeaking school as a speaker of a minority dialect (see Siegel, 2010)-the extent to which children adopt new ways of speaking (and in which situations) will depend in part on how strongly they wish to identify with speakers of those varieties, and on external pressures they may feel to adopt or resist it (e.g., Fordham, 1998; Starr, 2019; see also Berthele, 2002; Standford, 2008).
text.formatted: And when children encounter an entirely new language variety-for example by moving to a region with a different dialect or entering a standardspeaking school as a speaker of a minority dialect (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Siegel, 2010)</ref>-the extent to which children adopt new ways of speaking (and in which situations) will depend in part on how strongly they wish to identify with speakers of those varieties, and on external pressures they may feel to adopt or resist it (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Fordham, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Starr, 2019</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Berthele, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Standford, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Children not only selectively align with the language of others over longer periods of time, but also in moment-to-moment interactions.

While, generally speaking, children's language has been shown to become more similar to their interlocutor's across multiple levels of language-for example, phonetically (St. Pierre et al., 2022), lexically (Branigan et al., 2016), and syntactically (Branigan & Messenger, 2016)-through what is thought to be largely automatic processes (Pickering & Garrod, 2004), recent work has shown that children prefer to selectively align with members of their own social groups more than members of other groups.
text.formatted: While, generally speaking, children's language has been shown to become more similar to their interlocutor's across multiple levels of language-for example, phonetically <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(St. Pierre et al., 2022)</ref>, lexically <ref type="bibr">(Branigan et al., 2016)</ref>, and syntactically <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Branigan & Messenger, 2016)</ref>-through what is thought to be largely automatic processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Pickering & Garrod, 2004)</ref>, recent work has shown that children prefer to selectively align with members of their own social groups more than members of other groups.

text.text: In one recent study, St. Pierre et al. (2024) found that children were more likely to adopt the labels used by fellow in-group members, even when this meant using term they would not normally choose-saying sofa, for example, instead of the community preferred term couch.
text.formatted: In one recent study, <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">St. Pierre et al. (2024)</ref> found that children were more likely to adopt the labels used by fellow in-group members, even when this meant using term they would not normally choose-saying sofa, for example, instead of the community preferred term couch.

text.text: Strikingly, this effect was observed despite children being assigned to an ad hoc, minimal group (red or green team), demonstrating that even a newly formed group, with no prior meaning or familiarity, is enough to influence who children align their speech to.
Such socially selective linguistic alignment may stem from children's expectations about how individuals, as members of different social groups, should behave and relate to one another.

Children expect members of the same group to share traits, behaviors, and preferences (Jordan & Dunham, 2021; Rhodes et al., 2012), including how they speak (Liberman et al., 2017), and they sometimes expect members of different groups to act (and speak) in distinct ways (Oostenbroek & Over, 2015; Weatherhead & White, 2021).
text.formatted: Children expect members of the same group to share traits, behaviors, and preferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Jordan & Dunham, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Rhodes et al., 2012)</ref>, including how they speak <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Liberman et al., 2017)</ref>, and they sometimes expect members of different groups to act (and speak) in distinct ways <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Oostenbroek & Over, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Weatherhead & White, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, they expect members of a group to conform to group norms (Schmidt et al., 2012), and will disapprove of those who deviate from from them (Foster-Hanson et al., 2021; Roberts et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Additionally, they expect members of a group to conform to group norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Schmidt et al., 2012)</ref>, and will disapprove of those who deviate from from them <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Foster-Hanson et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Roberts et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Because being in a group means behaving like its members, aligning with others may serve not only to reaffirm group membership but also to establish or lay claim to it in the first place.

Indeed, children tend to imitate, conform, and align more-including speaking more like those around them-when they feel ostracized (e.g., Cordonier et al., 2018; Hopkins & Branigan, 2020; Over & Carpenter, 2009; Watson-Jones et al., 2016), suggesting that children align with others as a way to connect or affiliate with them (Hopkins & Branigan, 2020) and gain social/group approval (Giles et al., 2023; Wynn et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Indeed, children tend to imitate, conform, and align more-including speaking more like those around them-when they feel ostracized (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cordonier et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hopkins & Branigan, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Over & Carpenter, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Watson-Jones et al., 2016)</ref>, suggesting that children align with others as a way to connect or affiliate with them <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hopkins & Branigan, 2020)</ref> and gain social/group approval <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Giles et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Wynn et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Speaking like the members of a group, in other words, is one of the ways children can claim and reinforce their belonging to it.
The above discussion has only considered how individuals align their speech with a single individual or group.

In reality, however, children, like adults, do not associate or identify with just one group, but hold many social identities at once, each more or less relevant in a given situation (Gaither, 2018; Kang & Bodenhausen, 2015).
text.formatted: In reality, however, children, like adults, do not associate or identify with just one group, but hold many social identities at once, each more or less relevant in a given situation <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Gaither, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Kang & Bodenhausen, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: As they develop, they become increasingly aware of-and are able to reflect upon-their own multiple identities (Gaither et al., 2020), and to reason about the multiple (Mandalaywala & Legaspi, 2023) and intersecting (e.g., race × gender; Lei et al., 2020) identities of others.
text.formatted: As they develop, they become increasingly aware of-and are able to reflect upon-their own multiple identities <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gaither et al., 2020)</ref>, and to reason about the multiple <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Mandalaywala & Legaspi, 2023)</ref> and intersecting (e.g., race × gender; <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Lei et al., 2020)</ref> identities of others.

text.text: When evaluating others, children weigh competing group cues against one another, prioritizing some categories over others, favoring, for example, same-accented, other race peers over other-accented, same race peers (Kinzler et al., 2009; see also Arredondo et al., 2025; Kinzler et al., 2010).
text.formatted: When evaluating others, children weigh competing group cues against one another, prioritizing some categories over others, favoring, for example, same-accented, other race peers over other-accented, same race peers <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Kinzler et al., 2009</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Arredondo et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kinzler et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: How does this play out in children's own language production?
Whose speech do they take up when they belong to several groups at once?

In adults, speakers draw on the communicative styles of the groups they belong to, constructing distinctive, context-sensitive ways of speaking that reflect their multifaceted identities (e.g., Holliday, 2024; Podesva et al., 2012); yet very little is known about how children's language is shaped by their complex identities.
text.formatted: In adults, speakers draw on the communicative styles of the groups they belong to, constructing distinctive, context-sensitive ways of speaking that reflect their multifaceted identities (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Holliday, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Podesva et al., 2012)</ref>; yet very little is known about how children's language is shaped by their complex identities.

text.text: While previous work has shown that children align their language with in-group members from one social category (St. Pierre et al., 2024), it is unclear whether and how children's linguistic alignment is influenced by the multiple groups which they belong to, especially when these groups pull them towards different ways of speaking.
text.formatted: While previous work has shown that children align their language with in-group members from one social category <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(St. Pierre et al., 2024)</ref>, it is unclear whether and how children's linguistic alignment is influenced by the multiple groups which they belong to, especially when these groups pull them towards different ways of speaking.

text.text: Do children align more strongly with one of their groups than another, or does a competing membership weaken-or even reverse-the alignment seen when their memberships agree?
To investigate the influence of multiple group memberships on children's lexical alignment, we adapted the method used by St. Pierre et al. (2024).
text.formatted: To investigate the influence of multiple group memberships on children's lexical alignment, we adapted the method used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">St. Pierre et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: During the experiment, children were assigned to a team (green or yellow), and then participated in a virtual trivia-style game they believed involved five other children: two on their own team and three on the opposing team (in reality, all other players were pre-recorded and controlled by the experimenter).

In critical trials, where questions had multiple possible answers (e.g., chalkboard or blackboard), children heard the two members from their team respond with one label, and two members from the other team respond with the other before answering themselves.
As in St. Pierre et al. (2024), we manipulated whether children's teammates always produced the term preferred by the broader community or the dispreferred term (established by prior norming).
text.formatted: As in <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">St. Pierre et al. (2024)</ref>, we manipulated whether children's teammates always produced the term preferred by the broader community or the dispreferred term (established by prior norming).

text.text: In addition, we manipulated-though never explicitly mentioned-the gender of the (virtual) players, gender being among the earliest-emerging and most salient social categories in childhood (Martin & Ruble, 2004 , 2010), influencing who they prefer, imitate, trust and help (e.g., Shutts et al., 2010; Taylor, 2013; Wang et al., 2021; Weller & Lagattuta, 2014).
text.formatted: In addition, we manipulated-though never explicitly mentioned-the gender of the (virtual) players, gender being among the earliest-emerging and most salient social categories in childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Martin & Ruble, 2004</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">, 2010)</ref>, influencing who they prefer, imitate, trust and help (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Shutts et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Taylor, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wang et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Weller & Lagattuta, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: For half of the participants, their teammates shared their gender and their opponents did not (congruent group condition), and for the other half, their opponents shared their gender and their teammates did not (incongruent group condition).

Thus, in the incongruent group condition, children's teammates and their same-gender peers belonged to opposing teams, and therefore produced different terms, meaning that children were faced with the choice of using the label produced by their teammates, or the label produced by their same-gendered peers.

In the congruent group condition, where children shared both team membership and gender with their teammates, we expected to replicate St. Pierre et al. (2024), with children lexically aligning with their in-group, and producing dispreferred terms more often when their teammates did compared to when their teammates produced preferred terms.
text.formatted: In the congruent group condition, where children shared both team membership and gender with their teammates, we expected to replicate <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">St. Pierre et al. (2024)</ref>, with children lexically aligning with their in-group, and producing dispreferred terms more often when their teammates did compared to when their teammates produced preferred terms.

text.text: Critically, we predicted that this alignment would be modulated by gender, and that in the incongruent group condition, where the two group cues conflict, lexical alignment with teammates would be reduced or reversed depending on how children weigh the two membership cues.

If children consider both the labels of their teammates and same-gendered peers, they should align with their teammates on some trials and with their same-gender peers (i.e., their 'opponents') on others, weakening the overall alignment effect relative to the congruent condition.

If instead children prioritize gender membership over minimal group membership (see Yang et al., 2022), they should diverge from their teammates altogether, producing the dispreferred term more often when their teammates used the preferred term than when their teammates used the dispreferred one, the reverse of the pattern in the congruent condition.
text.formatted: If instead children prioritize gender membership over minimal group membership (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Yang et al., 2022)</ref>, they should diverge from their teammates altogether, producing the dispreferred term more often when their teammates used the preferred term than when their teammates used the dispreferred one, the reverse of the pattern in the congruent condition.

text.text: Crucially, we predict that children will behave differently in the congruent and incongruent conditions, considering their membership in multiple groups when deciding who to lexically align with.

We set a stopping rule of 128 children with usable data (64 girls, 64 boys), more than the 72 in St. Pierre et al. (2024), to account for our added gender manipulation (note that their power simulation for a control study indicated that 24 participants sufficed for detecting children's alignment with their in-group when only a single group cue, team membership, was present).

(2024)</ref>, to account for our added gender manipulation (note that their power simulation for a control study indicated that 24 participants sufficed for detecting children's alignment with their in-group when only a single group cue, team membership, was present).

text.text: The final sample-recruited from a lab database of families who previously indicated interest in participating in studies-included 7-to 9-year old children (MAGE = 8.18; SD = 0.81 Range = 6.96 -9.96) from the Greater Toronto Area, who were exposed to English at least 80% of the time, had no hearing/vision difficulties, and had at least one parent raised in an English speaking home in Canada.
Based on parental report, all children (64 boys and 64 girls) tested were cisgender.
The experimenters included four undergraduate women, all of whom grew up speaking the local variety of Canadian English.
Nine additional participants were tested but excluded due to technical issues (n = 4), caregiver interference (n = 1), and children having 50% or less usable trials (n = 4).

We tested an ethnically diverse sample, reflective of Toronto, where 57% identify as members of racialized groups, the largest being South Asian (19.2%), Chinese (11.1%), and Black (7.9%) (Statistics Canada, 2024).

Of the 93% of caregivers who reported on caregiver education (119/128), 75% reported both caregivers having a postsecondary degree (54 with university or postgraduate degrees, five with college [i.e., vocational] degrees, and 30 with one college and one university or postgraduate degree), 23% reported one caregiver completing a college or university degree (six college and 30 university or post graduate), and the remaining 3% reported no caregivers having a postsecondary degree.

Most children came from middle to upper middle class families; of the 70% of caregivers who provided information on household income (90/128), 53% reported a family income of over $140,000 CAD (~$100,000 USD), 36% an income between $90,000 (~65,000 USD) and $140,000, and the remaining 11% an income below $90,000 (note that the media household income in Toronto in 2020 was $84,000 CAD; Statistics Canada, 2023).
Based on previous norming (see St. Pierre et al., 2024), we selected 12 pairs of words that were familiar to 7-to 9-year-old children and could refer to the same objects (e.g., gift/present).
text.formatted: Based on previous norming (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">St. Pierre et al., 2024)</ref>, we selected 12 pairs of words that were familiar to 7-to 9-year-old children and could refer to the same objects (e.g., gift/present).

text.text: One of the two names in each pair was preferred by children in the community, being spontaneously produced by children more than 70% of the time in the norming experiment (see Appendix A for complete list of words).

Twelve questions were created to elicit these word pairs in a trivia game (e.g., What do kids often get on their birthday?), along with an additional 12 filler questions for distractor trials (e.g., What do you call a doctor for animals?
; see Appendix B).
Recordings of Canadian English-speaking children producing the answers to these questions were inserted into a trivia game created in PowerPoint (see St. Pierre et al., 2024 for more information).

text.text: The experiment was conducted online on Adobe Connect and consisted of two phases.

In the first phase (team assignment), children were told they were going to play in a trivia game on either the green team or the yellow team, but that first, the experimenter needed to figure out which team to assign them to.

To do this, the experimenter asked children about their preferences (e.g., whether they liked cats or dogs better, pizza or French fries, ice cream or chips, etc.), and told them they would be put on a team with children who shared their preferences (in actuality, children were assigned to a team color that their parents indicated during screening that their children preferred, as in St. Pierre et al., 2024).
text.formatted: To do this, the experimenter asked children about their preferences (e.g., whether they liked cats or dogs better, pizza or French fries, ice cream or chips, etc.), and told them they would be put on a team with children who shared their preferences (in actuality, children were assigned to a team color that their parents indicated during screening that their children preferred, as in <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">St. Pierre et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the second phase (trivia game), children entered a virtual room to play a trivia game that they believed involved two fellow teammates and three children from the opposing team (in fact, other children's responses were pre-recorded, experimenter-controlled audio files).

In the virtual room, each child was represented with an avatar (silhouette) of a boy or girl with a colored shirt-yellow or green, depending on their team color-containing their initials (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: In the virtual room, each child was represented with an avatar (silhouette) of a boy or girl with a colored shirt-yellow or green, depending on their team color-containing their initials (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: For half of the participants, their teammates matched them in gender (congruent group condition), while their opponents mismatched them; for the other half of participants, their teammates mismatched them in gender (incongruent group condition), while their opponents matched them.
This was signaled primarily by the children's avatars (male or female), but also by the fact that the child voices assigned to each avatar matched the gender of the avatar.
The participant's team was always positioned on the left-hand side of the screen, with the participant in the bottom left-hand corner.

To make it more believable that the other children were live rather than prerecorded, the experimenter first asked everyone to introduce themselves by stating their initials, whether they were joining on a computer or a tablet, and whether they were an ice cream person or a chip person (i.e., whether they had answered ice cream or chips in the team assignment phase; see St.
Pierre et al., 2024 for more details).
Then, the experimenter facilitated a trivia game consisting of six rounds of three questions (18 questions total).
Each round began with two filler trials, where one child from each team was called upon to answer a general trivia question, followed by a critical trial, where every child provided an answer.
In critical trials, participants always answered fifth, after both of their teammates and two members of the opposing team provided answers.
For half of the participants, their teammates always produced used preferred terms (e.g., present), while the other team used dispreferred terms (e.g., gift); for the other half, this was reversed.

Of interest was whether children would be more likely to produce dispreferred terms when their teammates did as well, and whether this depended on whether their teammates matched or mismatched their gender.

text.text: The study was conducted, and consent was obtained, in accordance with our ethics protocol, approved by the University of Toronto Ethics Board.
Altogether, we had a total of 764 responses (two of the 128 children only completed the first four trials).

After removing 4% of responses in which children didn't know the answer (N = 2) or provided either both the preferred and dispreferred term (e.g., icing and frosting; N = 11), or a third term (e.g., floatie instead of life jacket or life vest; N = 15), we were left with 736 responses.

The data were analyzed using a mixed effects logistic regression in the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) in R (R Core Team, 2026), predicting the likelihood of producing dispreferred labels from teammate label (i.e., whether teammates produced preferred or dispreferred labels), group congruence (i.e., whether teammates matched or mismatched the participant's gender), and their interaction.

text.text: To understand the nature of this interaction, we examined the simple effect of group congruence when teammates produced the preferred term (preferred recoded 0, and dispreferred 1) and when teammates produced the dispreferred term (preferred recoded 1, and dispreferred 0).

When teammates produced dispreferred labels, children were significantly more likely to also use dispreferred labels when their teammates matched their gender compared to when they mismatched (Bgender matching = 1.63, SE = 0.54, z = 3.02, p = .002, OR = 5.12, 95% CI [1.77, 14.77]).

In contrast, when teammates produced preferred labels, children were less likely to produce dispreferred labels when teammates matched their gender (Bgender matching = -0.79 , SE = 0.40, z = -1.98, p = .047, OR = 0.46, 95% CI [0.21, 0.99]).
In other words, children were more likely to lexically align with their teammates (i.e., produce the same labels as them) when those members matched their gender.

text.text: To test this, we reran our model adding child gender (boys, coded -0.5, girls, 0.5) and its interactions with group congruence and teammate label.

Results showed no evidence of a threeway interaction between child gender, group congruence, and teammate label (B = -1.92, SE = 1.32, z = -1.46, p = .15, OR = 0.15, 95% CI [0.01, 1.95]), suggesting that the interaction we observed between teammate label and group congruence did not differ between boys and girls.

Re-fitting the model with each gender as the reference level, we did find a significant team label × group congruence interaction for girls (B = -3.25, SE = 0.93, z = -3.49, p < .001, OR = 0.04, 95% CI [0.01, 0.24]) but not boys (B = -1.33, SE = 0.94, z = -1.41, p = .16, OR = 0.26, 95% CI [0.04, 1.69]), suggesting that the effect we observed may be driven to some extent by the girls, who showed stronger alignment in the congruent condition compared to the incongruent condition, whereas boys tended to align with their teammates, regardless of whether they mismatched their gender or not (see Figure 3).

People use language to signal to others which groups they belong to, partly by speaking like, or aligning with, other members of those groups.
But we rarely belong to just one group, and must learn to use language to signal our membership in multiple categories, even when those groups may have conflicting styles of speech.

In the current study, we asked whether 7-to 9year-old children's lexical choices (i.e., who they align with) are influenced by the multiple social categories that they belong to, especially when their multiple groups-in this case, their assigned teammates and same-gender peers-used different labels.

In line with previous work (St. Pierre et al., 2024), we found that children selectively aligned their language with their assigned in-group (i.e., their teammates), producing labels more like those of their teammates than of their opponents.
text.formatted: In line with previous work <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(St. Pierre et al., 2024)</ref>, we found that children selectively aligned their language with their assigned in-group (i.e., their teammates), producing labels more like those of their teammates than of their opponents.

text.text: Specifically, children were more likely to produce labels dispreferred by the broader community (e.g., sofa instead of couch) when their teammates produced dispreferred labels.

Given that children heard each label (preferred and dispreferred) the same number of times, and always heard an out-group member immediately before responding, children's preference for in-group labels cannot be explained by automatic, low-level processes (e.g., activation and recency; Pickering & Garrod, 2004), but by a socially selective process tied to children's group affiliation (Wynn et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Given that children heard each label (preferred and dispreferred) the same number of times, and always heard an out-group member immediately before responding, children's preference for in-group labels cannot be explained by automatic, low-level processes (e.g., activation and recency; <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Pickering & Garrod, 2004)</ref>, but by a socially selective process tied to children's group affiliation <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Wynn et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Most notably, children did not rely on a single group membership when deciding whose language to emulate, but at the same time weighed labels used by both their teammates and same-gender peers.

This was seen most clearly in the incongruent condition where team membership and gender membership were pitted against one another (i.e., when children's opposing team had same-gender peers and their own team other-gender peers).
In this condition, when teammates did not share the child's gender, their tendency to align with their teammates was attenuated compared to when their teammates matched their gender.
Specifically, they adopted their teammates' labels to a lesser extent, and opted instead to sometimes use the contrasting label produced by same gender peers on the opposite team.
To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that children's lexical alignment is sensitive to the communication patterns of the multiple groups that children belong to.
This particular pattern of results is notable for several reasons.

First, rather than categorically aligning with either their teammates or same gender peers on the opposing team, children in the incongruent condition appeared to integrate competing cues in a graded fashion, aligning to some extent with both groups.

This is seen both at the group level, where alignment was attenuated by conflicting gender cues rather than reversed (or unchanged from the congruent condition), and also on an individual level, with no evidence of a bimodal distribution of alignment (i.e., children either wholly aligning with one group or the other).

This suggests that children do not treat their group memberships as mutually exclusive, but, like adults (e.g., Holliday, 2024; Podesva et al., 2012), can hold and act on more than one membership at the same time through their language use.
text.formatted: This suggests that children do not treat their group memberships as mutually exclusive, but, like adults (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Holliday, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Podesva et al., 2012)</ref>, can hold and act on more than one membership at the same time through their language use.

text.text: Although the children in our study made a simple choice between two labels, their behavior may reflect an early capacity to simultaneously index more than one aspect of their identity in their speech.

Second, although children acknowledged both group memberships at once, they nevertheless did weigh one more heavily than the other, specifically team membership over gender, despite previous research suggesting that children prioritize gender over minimal groups (e.g., Yang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Second, although children acknowledged both group memberships at once, they nevertheless did weigh one more heavily than the other, specifically team membership over gender, despite previous research suggesting that children prioritize gender over minimal groups (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Yang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Part of this may reflect the fact that gender was never explicitly foregrounded in the experiment.

Whereas team membership was overtly established-children were assigned to a colored team of (ostensibly) like-minded peers, and the task was framed as a competition between these different colored teams-gender was conveyed only incidentally through each player's avatar and recorded voice.
This experimental emphasis on team membership (rather than gender membership) may have prompted children to generally align more with their teammates than same-gender peers.

Work with adults has shown that speakers are more likely to speak in ways that are characteristic of a particular part of their identity if they are in a context that primes or foregrounds that part of their identity (e.g., Hay et al., 2010; see Levon & Katsiveli, 2023).
text.formatted: Work with adults has shown that speakers are more likely to speak in ways that are characteristic of a particular part of their identity if they are in a context that primes or foregrounds that part of their identity (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hay et al., 2010</ref>; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Levon & Katsiveli, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For example, in one study, biracial adults were perceived as sounding more Black when previously primed to talk about their Black parent and more White when previously primed to talk about their White parent (Gaither et al., 2015).
text.formatted: For example, in one study, biracial adults were perceived as sounding more Black when previously primed to talk about their Black parent and more White when previously primed to talk about their White parent <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gaither et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Given that gender was never explicitly foregrounded in the experiment, it is in some ways striking that children's word choices were influenced by gender at all.

Future work manipulating the extent to which particular social categories are emphasized (e.g., making gender overt and team membership incidental) could help to establish the extent to which children's group-based alignment flexibly varies depending on how social categories are framed in particular contexts (see Wang et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Future work manipulating the extent to which particular social categories are emphasized (e.g., making gender overt and team membership incidental) could help to establish the extent to which children's group-based alignment flexibly varies depending on how social categories are framed in particular contexts (see <ref type="bibr">Wang et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, despite children's lexical choices being influenced by group membership, we should note that overall, children still tended to favor using the preferred term, even in the condition where their gender-matched teammates produced dispreferred terms.
In other words, children did not fully align with the dispreferred labels of their teammates, but continued producing preferred labels much of the time.

This is consistent with prior work showing that children produce preferred terms to a considerable degree even after exposure to dispreferred labels (Branigan et al., 2016; Hopkins & Branigan, 2020; Hopkins et al., 2017; St. Pierre et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This is consistent with prior work showing that children produce preferred terms to a considerable degree even after exposure to dispreferred labels <ref type="bibr">(Branigan et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hopkins & Branigan, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Hopkins et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">St. Pierre et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Whereas previous work might explain this as a matter of activation, where the priming of dispreferred terms does not always overcome the higher baseline activation of preferred terms, leading to occasional productions of preferred terms, we find it unlikely that the overall preference for preferred labels in our data is completely reducible to low level processes.

Instead, given that children heard both labels and were prompted to think about and produce their own response, we think that children continued to sometimes produce preferred terms by choice; however, the reasons why remain unclear.

One possibility is that children sometimes preferred the label that they would normally use, despite their teammates using another label, raising questions about how children balance the pressure or desire to conform to their group members while still "being themselves."

Another possibility is that children recognized that some labels are more frequent and conventional in the broader community than others, and were sometimes reluctant to follow teammates when they deviated from community norms (Rutland et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2012), raising the possibility that children were responding not only to their team and gender, but to a third group (i.e., the broader speech community whose conventions the preferred term reflects).

text.text: Future work should examine the extent to which children perceive dispreferred variants to be unconventional and 'marked' (Clark, 1990), and how that influences how they interpret individuals who produce these forms (see Diesendruck et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Future work should examine the extent to which children perceive dispreferred variants to be unconventional and 'marked' <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Clark, 1990)</ref>, and how that influences how they interpret individuals who produce these forms (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Diesendruck et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In sum, the current study shows that by middle childhood, children already track more than one of their group memberships at once and weigh them against each other in deciding whose speech to align with.
To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that children's lexical alignment is shaped by the language choices of group members from different social categories.
How this capacity emerges and scales up in more real-world contexts remains an open and important question at the intersection of developmental and sociolinguistic research.
